## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

"""T-601 — request and response shapes for the API.

`PROJECT_PLAN §7.2`. Deliberately thin: the pipeline already writes typed
artefacts to ``outputs/runs/<run_id>/``, so these models mostly describe how
those files are surfaced rather than inventing a second representation of the
same data.

⚠️ **The artefact directory is the source of truth, not a database.** Phase 6B
(T-620..T-626) adds a Postgres run registry, but `T-625` requires
``GET /api/runs`` to work with no database at all, falling back to a filesystem
scan. Building against the filesystem first is therefore not a shortcut - it is
the contract the registry has to preserve.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Any

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class ReviewRequest(BaseModel):
    """``POST /api/review``."""

    question: str = Field(min_length=10)
    #: Defaults to the configured value when omitted. The ceiling matches the
    #: largest size Panel 1 offers (T-611) - a picker whose top entry the API
    #: rejects is worse than no picker, and at le=60 that is exactly what
    #: choosing 100 did.
    #:
    #: ⚠️ The ceiling is a REQUEST bound, not a promise about runtime. Cost is
    #: roughly linear in max_papers and is paced by the provider's tokens per
    #: minute, not by CPU: measured 2026-08-29, extraction admits about one
    #: paper a minute on Groq's free tier, so 100 papers is ~100 minutes of
    #: extraction alone and ~650,000 reserved tokens against a 200,000/day
    #: budget - i.e. it cannot finish in one day. Panel 1 says so next to the
    #: sizes it offers; this bound only stops the request being absurd.
    max_papers: int | None = Field(default=None, ge=1, le=100)
    #: Run the six-agent graph (Verifier + Critic) rather than the M1 line.
    use_loop: bool = True


class ReviewAccepted(BaseModel):
    """``POST /api/review`` -> 202. The run has *started*, not finished."""

    run_id: str
    events_url: str
    result_url: str


class RunSummary(BaseModel):
    """One row of ``GET /api/runs``."""

    run_id: str
    status: str                      # running | complete | failed
    question: str | None = None
    started: str | None = None
    papers: int | None = None
    verified_claims: int | None = None
    dropped_claims: int | None = None
    grounding_score: float | None = None
    artefacts: list[str] = []


class EvidenceOut(BaseModel):
    chunk_id: str
    quote: str


class ClaimOut(BaseModel):
    """A verified or dropped claim, with what justified the verdict.

    ★ ``evidence`` is what makes Panel 3 (T-607) possible: click a sentence,
    see the span the Verifier actually scored it against. Returning a verdict
    without its evidence would make the panel a claim about the system rather
    than a demonstration of it.
    """

    claim_id: str
    text: str
    verdict: str
    support_score: float
    paper_ids: list[str] = []
    evidence: list[EvidenceOut] = []


class OverrideRequest(BaseModel):
    """``POST /api/runs/{id}/overrides`` — T-609.

    ⚠️ This records a human judgement ABOUT a dropped claim. It does not edit
    the review, and it must not: putting dropped prose back into ``review.md``
    on a click would destroy the very property the panel exists to demonstrate.
    """

    claim_id: str = Field(min_length=1)
    #: ``confirm``  - the Verifier was right to drop it
    #: ``reinstate`` - a human disagrees and would have kept it
    #: ``null``     - clear a previous override (a mis-click must be undoable)
    decision: str | None = None
    note: str | None = Field(default=None, max_length=2000)


class OverrideOut(BaseModel):
    claim_id: str
    decision: str | None = None
    note: str | None = None
    ts: str | None = None


class RunResult(BaseModel):
    """``GET /api/runs/{id}/result`` — everything the Vue app renders."""

    run_id: str
    status: str
    question: str | None = None
    review_markdown: str = ""
    grounding_score: float | None = None
    counts: dict[str, Any] = {}
    verified_claims: list[ClaimOut] = []
    #: Kept in the same payload as the verified ones, deliberately. Panel 4
    #: exists to show what the system REFUSED to say, and that is only
    #: persuasive next to what it did say.
    dropped_claims: list[ClaimOut] = []
    papers: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
    artefacts: list[str] = []
    decisions: list[str] = []
    iterations: int = 0
    #: T-609. Reconstructed from the trace, so a reload shows what a
    #: human already decided.
    human_overrides: list[OverrideOut] = []


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# T-612 — human scoring
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

#: 1 is worst, 5 is best. Mirrors the CHECK constraint in ``db/models.py`` -
#: validated in both places on purpose, so a score written by psql or by a
#: later script is still in range.
SCORE_MIN, SCORE_MAX = 1, 5


class PaperScoreIn(BaseModel):
    """One reviewer judgement of one paper the Extractor read."""

    #: The pipeline's identity for the paper, not its DOI: about one OpenAlex
    #: record in five has no DOI, and those papers must still be scoreable.
    paper_id: str = Field(min_length=1)
    score: int = Field(ge=SCORE_MIN, le=SCORE_MAX)
    note: str | None = Field(default=None, max_length=2000)


class ArtefactScoreIn(BaseModel):
    """The reviewer's verdict on the generated review itself."""

    score: int = Field(ge=SCORE_MIN, le=SCORE_MAX)
    note: str | None = Field(default=None, max_length=2000)
    artefact: str = "review.md"


class ScoreSubmission(BaseModel):
    """``POST /api/runs/{id}/scores`` — T-612.

    Scoring the papers and scoring the write-up are deliberately separate
    fields rather than one number: they answer "was retrieval any good?" and
    "was the writing any good?", and the automated metrics cannot currently
    tell those apart.
    """

    papers: list[PaperScoreIn] = Field(default_factory=list)
    artefact: ArtefactScoreIn | None = None


class ScoredPaper(BaseModel):
    """A row of the review sheet: what to judge, plus any judgement so far."""

    paper_id: str
    doi: str | None = None
    title: str
    venue: str | None = None
    year: int | None = None
    url: str | None = None
    score: int | None = None
    note: str | None = None


class ArtefactInfo(BaseModel):
    name: str
    chars: int


class ScoreSheet(BaseModel):
    """``GET /api/runs/{id}/scores`` and the reply to a submission."""

    run_id: str
    papers: list[ScoredPaper]
    artefact: ArtefactInfo | None = None
    artefact_score: ArtefactScoreIn | None = None
    #: ``"trace"`` or ``"trace+db"``. The UI shows the difference rather than
    #: claiming a database write that did not happen - the registry is
    #: best-effort (`DB_SCHEMA.md §9`) and may simply be absent.
    persisted: str = "trace"


__all__ = [
    "ReviewRequest",
    "OverrideRequest",
    "OverrideOut",
    "ReviewAccepted",
    "RunSummary",
    "ClaimOut",
    "EvidenceOut",
    "RunResult",
    "PaperScoreIn",
    "ArtefactScoreIn",
    "ScoreSubmission",
    "ScoredPaper",
    "ArtefactInfo",
    "ScoreSheet",
    "SCORE_MIN",
    "SCORE_MAX",
]

"""T-601 — request and response shapes for the API.

`PROJECT_PLAN §7.2`. Deliberately thin: the pipeline already writes typed
artefacts to ``outputs/runs/<run_id>/``, so these models mostly describe how
those files are surfaced rather than inventing a second representation of the
same data.

⚠️ **The artefact directory is the source of truth, not a database.** Phase 6B
(T-620..T-626) adds a Postgres run registry, but `T-625` requires
``GET /api/runs`` to work with no database at all, falling back to a filesystem
scan. Building against the filesystem first is therefore not a shortcut - it is
the contract the registry has to preserve.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Any

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class ReviewRequest(BaseModel):
    """``POST /api/review``."""

    question: str = Field(min_length=10)
    #: Defaults to the configured value when omitted. The ceiling matches the
    #: largest size Panel 1 offers (T-611) - a picker whose top entry the API
    #: rejects is worse than no picker, and at le=60 that is exactly what
    #: choosing 100 did.
    #:
    #: ⚠️ The ceiling is a REQUEST bound, not a promise about runtime. Cost is
    #: roughly linear in max_papers and is paced by the provider's tokens per
    #: minute, not by CPU: measured 2026-08-29, extraction admits about one
    #: paper a minute on Groq's free tier, so 100 papers is ~100 minutes of
    #: extraction alone and ~650,000 reserved tokens against a 200,000/day
    #: budget - i.e. it cannot finish in one day. Panel 1 says so next to the
    #: sizes it offers; this bound only stops the request being absurd.
    max_papers: int | None = Field(default=None, ge=1, le=100)
    #: Run the six-agent graph (Verifier + Critic) rather than the M1 line.
    use_loop: bool = True


class ReviewAccepted(BaseModel):
    """``POST /api/review`` -> 202. The run has *started*, not finished."""

    run_id: str
    events_url: str
    result_url: str


class RunSummary(BaseModel):
    """One row of ``GET /api/runs``."""

    run_id: str
    status: str                      # running | complete | failed
    question: str | None = None
    started: str | None = None
    papers: int | None = None
    verified_claims: int | None = None
    dropped_claims: int | None = None
    grounding_score: float | None = None
    artefacts: list[str] = []


class EvidenceOut(BaseModel):
    chunk_id: str
    quote: str


class ClaimOut(BaseModel):
    """A verified or dropped claim, with what justified the verdict.

    ★ ``evidence`` is what makes Panel 3 (T-607) possible: click a sentence,
    see the span the Verifier actually scored it against. Returning a verdict
    without its evidence would make the panel a claim about the system rather
    than a demonstration of it.
    """

    claim_id: str
    text: str
    verdict: str
    support_score: float
    paper_ids: list[str] = []
    evidence: list[EvidenceOut] = []


class OverrideRequest(BaseModel):
    """``POST /api/runs/{id}/overrides`` — T-609.

    ⚠️ This records a human judgement ABOUT a dropped claim. It does not edit
    the review, and it must not: putting dropped prose back into ``review.md``
    on a click would destroy the very property the panel exists to demonstrate.
    """

    claim_id: str = Field(min_length=1)
    #: ``confirm``  - the Verifier was right to drop it
    #: ``reinstate`` - a human disagrees and would have kept it
    #: ``null``     - clear a previous override (a mis-click must be undoable)
    decision: str | None = None
    note: str | None = Field(default=None, max_length=2000)


class OverrideOut(BaseModel):
    claim_id: str
    decision: str | None = None
    note: str | None = None
    ts: str | None = None


class RunResult(BaseModel):
    """``GET /api/runs/{id}/result`` — everything the Vue app renders."""

    run_id: str
    status: str
    question: str | None = None
    review_markdown: str = ""
    grounding_score: float | None = None
    counts: dict[str, Any] = {}
    verified_claims: list[ClaimOut] = []
    #: Kept in the same payload as the verified ones, deliberately. Panel 4
    #: exists to show what the system REFUSED to say, and that is only
    #: persuasive next to what it did say.
    dropped_claims: list[ClaimOut] = []
    papers: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
    artefacts: list[str] = []
    decisions: list[str] = []
    iterations: int = 0
    #: T-609. Reconstructed from the trace, so a reload shows what a
    #: human already decided.
    human_overrides: list[OverrideOut] = []


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# T-612 — human scoring
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

#: 1 is worst, 5 is best. Mirrors the CHECK constraint in ``db/models.py`` -
#: validated in both places on purpose, so a score written by psql or by a
#: later script is still in range.
SCORE_MIN, SCORE_MAX = 1, 5


class PaperScoreIn(BaseModel):
    """One reviewer judgement of one paper the Extractor read."""

    #: The pipeline's identity for the paper, not its DOI: about one OpenAlex
    #: record in five has no DOI, and those papers must still be scoreable.
    paper_id: str = Field(min_length=1)
    score: int = Field(ge=SCORE_MIN, le=SCORE_MAX)
    note: str | None = Field(default=None, max_length=2000)


class ArtefactScoreIn(BaseModel):
    """The reviewer's verdict on the generated review itself."""

    score: int = Field(ge=SCORE_MIN, le=SCORE_MAX)
    note: str | None = Field(default=None, max_length=2000)
    artefact: str = "review.md"


class ScoreSubmission(BaseModel):
    """``POST /api/runs/{id}/scores`` — T-612.

    Scoring the papers and scoring the write-up are deliberately separate
    fields rather than one number: they answer "was retrieval any good?" and
    "was the writing any good?", and the automated metrics cannot currently
    tell those apart.
    """

    papers: list[PaperScoreIn] = Field(default_factory=list)
    artefact: ArtefactScoreIn | None = None


class ScoredPaper(BaseModel):
    """A row of the review sheet: what to judge, plus any judgement so far."""

    paper_id: str
    doi: str | None = None
    title: str
    venue: str | None = None
    year: int | None = None
    url: str | None = None
    score: int | None = None
    note: str | None = None


class ArtefactInfo(BaseModel):
    name: str
    chars: int


class ScoreSheet(BaseModel):
    """``GET /api/runs/{id}/scores`` and the reply to a submission."""

    run_id: str
    papers: list[ScoredPaper]
    artefact: ArtefactInfo | None = None
    artefact_score: ArtefactScoreIn | None = None
    #: ``"trace"`` or ``"trace+db"``. The UI shows the difference rather than
    #: claiming a database write that did not happen - the registry is
    #: best-effort (`DB_SCHEMA.md §9`) and may simply be absent.
    persisted: str = "trace"


__all__ = [
    "ReviewRequest",
    "OverrideRequest",
    "OverrideOut",
    "ReviewAccepted",
    "RunSummary",
    "ClaimOut",
    "EvidenceOut",
    "RunResult",
    "PaperScoreIn",
    "ArtefactScoreIn",
    "ScoreSubmission",
    "ScoredPaper",
    "ArtefactInfo",
    "ScoreSheet",
    "SCORE_MIN",
    "SCORE_MAX",
]

    🔴 **The filesystem is the BASE SET; the registry only enriches it.**
    The obvious implementation — "registry if present, else filesystem" — is

    Enabling an *index* must never make the application show less than reality

    So: enumerate the disk, then overlay registry metrics where a row exists.
    A registry row whose directory is gone is skipped — the artefacts are what

def _normalise(s: str) -> str:
    """Must stay identical to PanelEvidence.vue::normalise."""
    import re

def test_verified_claims_are_locatable_in_the_review():
    """Panel 3 highlights a sentence by matching NORMALISED text, not offsets.

    🔴 The Verifier strips `[n]` markers when it decomposes and the Writer's
    markdown carries them, so a byte offset into review.md points at the wrong
    place. If the two normalisations ever drift apart the panel silently
    highlights nothing and the graded "money shot" renders as plain prose -
    with no error anywhere. This asserts the contract from the Python side so a
    pipeline change cannot break the front end unnoticed.

    Measured on the fixture 2026-08-28: 19 of 19 claims located.

    import json
    import pathlib

    run = pathlib.Path("outputs/runs/fixture")

        pytest.skip("fixture not built in this checkout")

    review = (run / "review.md").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    verified = claims["verified"]

        f"review.md ({missing[:5]}). Panel 3 would highlight nothing."

#: What Panel 1 offers. A fixed list rather than a free number box: these are
#: the sizes whose cost is actually known (see the runtime note in the panel),
#: and a typed 8,347 is a two-hour run nobody meant to start.
MAX_PAPER_OPTIONS = (5, 10, 15, 25, 50, 100)


def test_t611_every_offered_size_is_accepted_by_the_api():
    """🔴 The bound was ``le=60`` while the panel now offers 100, so choosing
    the largest size would have 422'd - a picker that cannot pick its own top
    entry. This test exists to keep the two ends from drifting again."""
    import pydantic
    import pytest as _pytest

    from researchgpt.api.schemas import ReviewRequest

    question = "How do multi-agent systems reduce hallucination in reviews?"
    for size in MAX_PAPER_OPTIONS:
        assert ReviewRequest(question=question, max_papers=size).max_papers == size

    # The ceiling is still a ceiling: above the largest offered size it fails.
    with _pytest.raises(pydantic.ValidationError):
        ReviewRequest(question=question, max_papers=max(MAX_PAPER_OPTIONS) + 1)
    with _pytest.raises(pydantic.ValidationError):
        ReviewRequest(question=question, max_papers=0)


def test_t611_the_panel_offers_exactly_those_sizes():
    """The picker is the contract the test above checks. Read it from the
    component so the two cannot say different things."""
    import pathlib
    import re

    repo = pathlib.Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
    panel = (repo / "frontend" / "src" / "components" / "PanelRun.vue").read_text(
        encoding="utf-8")
    match = re.search(r"const PAPER_OPTIONS = \[([0-9,\s]+)\]", panel)
    assert match, "PanelRun.vue must declare PAPER_OPTIONS for this to be checkable"
    offered = tuple(int(n) for n in match.group(1).replace(" ", "").strip(",").split(","))
    assert offered == MAX_PAPER_OPTIONS

# ResearchGPT

**A multi-agent agentic RAG platform for automated literature review.**

Given a research question, ResearchGPT plans sub-questions, searches the
literature, ranks and extracts from what it finds, drafts a cited survey — and
then **verifies every claim it wrote against the evidence it retrieved, dropping
whatever it cannot ground.**

The last step is the point. Four independent measurements say a citation is
almost no evidence that a statement is supported:

| study | finding |
|---|---|
| Sarol et al. | 39.18% of citation instances contain accuracy errors |
| ALCE | best models "lack complete citation support 50% of the time" |
| FActScore | ChatGPT factually correct on 58% of atomic claims |
| SurveyGen | 35.84% citation accuracy |

FActScore's sharpest number: **36.0% of supported and 37.6% of unsupported
sentences carried citations — statistically indistinguishable.** The presence of
a citation carries almost no information. That is the justification for
claim-level verification.

G. Shashivadan Rao, P. Sreekaran Reddy.

## The architecture

```
                  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
                  ▼                                       │

                  ▲                                  │    │
                  │                                  ▼    │
                  └──── RETRIEVE / REPLAN ──── WRITER ──▶ VERIFIER
                                                           │
                                                          END
```

Six agents on a LangGraph state machine. The **Critic** is visited twice per
iteration: once after the Extractor, where its cheap gates run *before* the
Writer spends tokens, and again after the Verifier, where the grounding gate
finally has a score to read.

| agent | does | LLM? |
|---|---|---|
| Planner | question → 4–8 sub-questions + search plan | yes |
| Retriever | OpenAlex + arXiv, dedup by DOI then title | no |
| Ranker | embed, hybrid BM25+dense retrieval, cross-encoder rerank | no |
| Extractor | per paper: methodology, advantages, limitations, datasets, metrics | yes |
| Writer | thematic synthesis, evidence-first with `[n]` citations | yes |
| **Verifier** | atomic claims → NLI against retrieved evidence → **drop the ungrounded** | no (local ONNX) |
| Critic | coverage / corpus / grounding gates → `WRITE \| RETRIEVE \| REPLAN` | no |

every gate is arithmetic, and a loop that spends tokens deciding whether to
spend tokens is the worst place for a generative step. Claim decomposition is
rule-based for the same reason, plus a sharper one: a model in that seat can
*invent* a claim the draft never made.

Two fine-tuned models, ~66M parameters combined, both trained on free Kaggle
GPU and both deployed **quantized to int8 on a CPU-only machine**:

| model | params | trained on | metric | stock | fine-tuned |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Claim verifier (`deberta-v3-small`) | 44M | SciFact | held-out macro-F1 | 0.516 | **0.769** |
| Cross-encoder reranker (`MiniLM-L-6`) | 22M | SciReviewGen | Recall@20, own bibliography | 0.4815 | **0.5926** |

The generative agents are **not** fine-tuned, deliberately — see
`documents/TRAINING_SPEC.md §4`. The thesis is Valsci's: *architecture beats model scale*.
Small trained components at the two real bottlenecks (retrieval quality, claim
grounding) do more than a larger generator would.

### $0 by construction

Only free, open-weight models, enforced in code: `core/llm.py` checks an
`ALLOWED_MODELS` constant before any HTTP request is constructed. There is no
second line of defence, and that is intentional.

|---|---|

| `refs.bib` | BibTeX |

## Results, honestly

Measured on 2026-08-28. The weaknesses are stated here because they read far
worse when a reviewer finds them first.

**What works.** The full six-agent loop runs end to end, and the Critic loop
fires and terminates on real data. From `outputs/runs/fixture/` — the recorded
showcase run, and the one the demo replays:

| | |
|---|---|
| Critic decisions | `RETRIEVE → REPLAN → RETRIEVE → WRITE` |
| corpus | 271 → **551 papers** (the replan added 280) |
| claims decomposed | 22 |
| kept / dropped | 19 / 3 |
| grounding | 0.8636 |

the plan it replaced, and those queries doubled the corpus. Every kept claim
carries the evidence span it was scored against, and all 19 are locatable in the
rendered review — which is what makes the evidence panel a demonstration rather
than a claim.


def test_every_cited_paper_reaches_the_evidence_panel():
    """Panel 3 names a claim's SOURCE by resolving its ``paper_ids`` against
    the ``papers`` list in the same payload. So the payload's size cap must
    never drop a paper a claim cites.

    🔴 It did. The cap was a plain ``papers[:200]`` over a corpus in RETRIEVAL
    order, while the cited papers are whatever the Ranker floated to the top —
    unrelated orders. On the fixture, five of the nine cited papers sit at
    positions 251-466 and fell outside the slice, so more than half of the
    panel's source lookups missed and it could only say "not in this payload"
    about a paper the run had read. A slice is the obvious implementation and
    the wrong one; this test is what makes that visible.
    """
    import json
    import pathlib

    from researchgpt.api.app import RESULT_PAPER_LIMIT, _papers_for_panel

    run = pathlib.Path("outputs/runs/fixture")
    if not (run / "claims.json").exists():
        pytest.skip("fixture not built in this checkout")

    claims = json.loads((run / "claims.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    corpus = json.loads((run / "corpus.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))

    served = _papers_for_panel(corpus, claims)
    served_ids = {p["paper_id"] for p in served}

    cited = {
        pid
        for bucket in ("verified", "dropped")
        for claim in claims[bucket]
        for pid in claim.get("paper_ids") or []
    }
    known = {p["paper_id"] for p in corpus["papers"]}

    missing = (cited & known) - served_ids
    assert not missing, (
        f"{len(missing)} cited papers are absent from /result: {sorted(missing)[:5]}. "
        "Panel 3 cannot name their source."
    )

    # The papers a human is asked to score must survive the cap for the same
    # reason - and the cap itself has to still be a cap.
    extracted = set(corpus.get("extracted_paper_ids") or []) & known
    assert extracted <= served_ids, "extracted papers were truncated away"
    assert len(served) <= RESULT_PAPER_LIMIT
    assert len(served_ids) == len(served), "the payload repeats a paper"
'''

content.text:
Both background servers exited because I killed them — expected.

## What I did

The frontend was structurally sound but visually flat and, more importantly, **information-poor**: it was discarding most of what the backend already streamed to it.

### The root problem I found

`api.js` subscribed to 13 named SSE events. The server emits 21+. `EventSource` only delivers a named event to a listener registered for that exact name — so nine of the richest payloads were being silently dropped: the plan's sub-questions, every search query and what it returned, `rank_summary`, `extract_summary`, `review_written`, and the LLM request/cache counts. No error anywhere. That's now the filter it's documented as, enumerated from every event name in `src/researchgpt/` and every trace on disk.

**New `src/lib/runStats.js`** folds those events into one digest. Verified against `outputs/runs/fixture/` — it reproduces the README's numbers (551 papers, 22 claims, 19/3, 0.8636) plus a lot the UI never had: per-agent elapsed time, 68 search queries grouped by round, rerank cost, LLM cache hit rate, wall clock.

### Two real defects fixed

1. **`paperById` in PanelEvidence was computed and never read.** The "money shot" panel showed an evidence quote and a chunk id — a chunk id isn't a citation you can follow. It now names the paper with venue, year, citations and a DOI link.
2. **Serving that exposed an API bug.** `papers[:200]` sliced a corpus in *retrieval* order, while cited papers are wherever the Ranker floated them — unrelated orders. Five of the fixture's nine cited papers sat at positions 251–466 and fell outside the slice. `_papers_for_panel` now puts cited and extracted papers first. I added a regression test and confirmed it fails on the old code with exactly those 5 ids.

### New information on screen
- **Panel 0 · Run** — the question itself (previously nowhere on the page), status, wall clock, model, the Critic chain *with its reasons*, six stat tiles, a verdict-composition bar, and the token cost. It states plainly that 19 claims were capped at PARTIAL by design because the corpus is abstracts.
- **Panel 2 · Agents** — a stage rail with the one number per stage, every Critic gate's arithmetic, and a collapsible query log that computes the README's "12 new queries with zero repeats" claim *from the run in front of you*.
- **Panel 5 · Sources (new)** — the funnel: retrieved → read → cited. The corpus was in the payload and rendered nowhere on the main route.
- **Dropped claims** now show the closest evidence found, and the reviewer's *note* is finally sent (`OverrideRequest.note` accepted one all along; the UI never passed it).
- **Dashboard** — added the measured run, the two fine-tuned models with stock-vs-tuned bars, the `$0 by construction` constraint, the artefact table, and four honest limitations.

### UI/UX

content.text: Real bug: 68 of 80 runs use `question`, but the API only reads `research_question`. Fixing all three layers:

input.command:
cd "C:/Users/Sreekaran/Desktop/Major Project" && python - <<'PY'
import pathlib
p = pathlib.Path("src/researchgpt/api/app.py")
s = p.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
old = '''def _question_of(events: list[dict]) -> str | None:
    for e in events:
        if e.get("event") == "run_start":
            return (e.get("payload") or {}).get("research_question")
    return None
'''
new = '''#: The two keys a ``run_start`` payload can carry the question under. There are
#: genuinely two emitters and they never agreed: ``graph/build.py`` writes
#: ``research_question``, ``cli.py`` writes ``question``.
_QUESTION_KEYS = ("research_question", "question")


def _question_of(events: list[dict]) -> str | None:
    """The question a run was asked, from whichever emitter recorded it.

    🔴 This read ``research_question`` only, and returned on the FIRST
    ``run_start`` it saw. A CLI-launched run emits its own ``run_start`` first,
    under ``question`` — so the function hit that record, found no
    ``research_question``, and returned None. Measured 2026-08-30 across
    ``outputs/runs/``: **68 of 80 runs carry the CLI shape**, so the endpoint
    was blind to the question of 85% of runs on disk.

    That was invisible while the run picker led with the run id. It stopped
    being invisible the moment the picker led with the question, which is the
    only thing that distinguishes one run from another in a list of eighty.

    So: scan every ``run_start``, accept either key, and take the first one that
    actually has a question rather than the first record that merely looks like
    the right event.
    """
    for e in events:
        if e.get("event") != "run_start":
            continue
        payload = e.get("payload") or {}
        for key in _QUESTION_KEYS:
            value = payload.get(key)
            if isinstance(value, str) and value.strip():
                return value
    return None
'''
assert old in s
p.write_text(s.replace(old, new), encoding="utf-8")
print("app.py patched")
PY

11	//
12	// ⚠️ Pure and defensive on purpose. Events arrive from a stream that replays
13	// history, a live run delivers the same shapes half-finished, and old runs on
14	// disk predate fields added later — so every read is optional and every caller
15	// gets something it can render. A missing key must produce an em dash, never a

39	 * Fold a run's events into one digest.

41	 * Summaries that describe an ITERATION are summed: the Retriever runs again
42	 * after a REPLAN and reports only what that pass added. Summaries that describe
43	 * the run's current STATE — the ranking, the extraction, the draft, the
44	 * verification — take the latest, because an earlier one has been superseded

content.text: Screenshots keep timing out on scroll — that points at a repaint problem I introduced. `background-attachment: fixed` with a gradient forces a full repaint on every scroll frame:

input.command:
cd "C:/Users/Sreekaran/Desktop/Major Project/frontend" && python - <<'PY'
import pathlib
p = pathlib.Path("src/style.css")
s = p.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
old = """  /* A very soft accent wash behind the header. Enough to stop the page reading
     as a white rectangle; not enough to compete with anything on it. */
  background-image:
    radial-gradient(60rem 22rem at 50% -8rem, theme('colors.accent.soft'), transparent);
  background-repeat: no-repeat;
  background-attachment: fixed;
}"""
new = """  /* A very soft accent wash behind the header. Enough to stop the page reading
     as a white rectangle; not enough to compete with anything on it.
     ⚠️ NOT `background-attachment: fixed`. A fixed gradient has to be recomposited
     on every scroll frame, and on the run page — a long document plus a
     backdrop-blurred sticky header — that was enough to stall the renderer for
     seconds at a time. It scrolls with the page, which is also what a wash
     behind the header should do. */
  background-image:
    radial-gradient(60rem 22rem at 50% -8rem, theme('colors.accent.soft'), transparent);
  background-repeat: no-repeat;
}"""
assert old in s
p.write_text(s.replace(old, new), encoding="utf-8")
print("style.css patched")

# The sticky header's blur is the other per-frame cost; a lighter radius keeps
# the effect at a fraction of the work.
p = pathlib.Path("src/components/AppHeader.vue")
s = p.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
s = s.replace("bg-paper/80 backdrop-blur-md", "bg-paper/85 backdrop-blur-sm")
s = s.replace("dark:bg-night/80", "dark:bg-night/85")
p.write_text(s, encoding="utf-8")
print("AppHeader patched")

content.text: Found it — the inner grid's children lack `min-w-0`, so they can't shrink below their content's min-content width:

input.command:
cd "C:/Users/Sreekaran/Desktop/Major Project/frontend" && python - <<'PY'
import pathlib
p = pathlib.Path("src/App.vue")
s = p.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
old = '''        <div class="grid min-w-0 items-start gap-4 2xl:grid-cols-2">'''
new = '''        <!-- `[&>*]:min-w-0` is load-bearing, not cosmetic. A grid item defaults
             to `min-width: auto`, i.e. it refuses to shrink below its own
             min-content width — and these two panels contain nowrap `truncate`
             spans, whose min-content is the FULL untruncated string. At 375px
             that pushed the track to 466px and gave the whole page a horizontal
             scrollbar, while the panels in the flex column beside them were
             fine (a column flex container applies min-height, not min-width).
             Measured in a 390px frame, 2026-08-30. -->
        <div class="grid min-w-0 items-start gap-4 [&>*]:min-w-0 2xl:grid-cols-2">'''
assert old in s
p.write_text(s.replace(old, new), encoding="utf-8")
print("App.vue patched")
PY
npm run build 2>&1 | tail -3

Screenshot: `C:\Users\SREEKA~1\AppData\Local\Temp\claude-chrome-screenshots-xgQ1p1\screenshot-1788110354963-0.jpg`

## Visual verification found four more real bugs

Seeing it in a browser was worth it — the structural checks had all passed, but four defects only showed up on screen.

**1. Every previous run read "(question not recorded)".** A backend bug my redesign exposed: there are two `run_start` emitters that never agreed — `graph/build.py` writes `research_question`, `cli.py` writes `question`. `_question_of` read only the first key and returned on the *first* `run_start` it saw, which for a CLI run is the CLI one. **68 of 80 runs on disk carry the CLI shape**, so the endpoint was blind to 85% of questions. Invisible while the picker led with the run id; unmissable once it led with the question. Fixed in `app.py` and mirrored in `runStats.js`, with a fallback to the run id for genuinely question-less runs.

**2. Raw markdown in the review prose.** `**Formal multi-agent architectures.**` reached the screen with its asterisks — in the one panel whose job is to be read closely. Pre-existing, and ironic: the matching worked perfectly because `normalise()` strips `*` itself, which is exactly why nobody noticed the *display* didn't. Now rendered through `marked.parseInline`; the raw text is untouched, since that's what claims are matched against. Verified: **0 literal `**` anywhere**, 5 `<strong>` in prose.

**3. Horizontal scrollbar at 375px.** Grids declared `sm:grid-cols-2` with **no base `grid-cols-1`** — so below the breakpoint `grid-template-columns` is `none`, the implicit column is `auto`-sized, and it never clamps to its container. Combined with `truncate` spans (whose min-content is the *full untruncated string*), the Dropped/Sources track blew out to 466px inside a 343px column. Fixed in 8 places, plus `[&>*]:min-w-0` on the inner grid.

**4. `background-attachment: fixed`** on the body gradient — a per-frame recomposite I'd added. Removing it is correct practice, though I should correct my own diagnosis: it was *not* the cause of the screenshot timeouts. Those were extension flakiness — the page measured 16ms JS response and 1359 DOM nodes throughout.

## What I confirmed working

- **All 19 claims resolve a real source** — title, authors, venue, year, citation count, working DOI. That's the API cap fix landing (was 4 of 9).
- **The Critic's gates read as an argument**: `i1 REPLAN — 271 papers retained, below min_papers=5000 · a previous RETRIEVE left the corpus at 271 papers; searching harder is not working, so the plan is the problem` → `i2 RETRIEVE 551 papers`. That reasoning was previously only in a `title` attribute a screenshot can't show.
- Theme toggle across all three states (class, `localStorage`, `colorScheme`, `aria-checked`), `/optimizer` gating (7 panels, 55 score pips), model bars at 51.6/76.9/48.15/59.26% matching the README exactly.
- **Zero horizontal overflow at 390/768/1024/1440px on all three routes.**

Since window resizing didn't work in this environment, I tested responsiveness by probing the app in sized iframes — their viewport drives media queries, so the breakpoints were genuinely exercised.

**334 passed, 1 skipped** (up one — my new regression test). The two remaining ruff errors are pre-existing in `test_phase2_acceptance.py`, which I never touched. Nothing committed.
